text.title: RFC Template for Product Dev Team Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every RFC Template for Product Dev Team application MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `problem` that names the current state with a measured value (for example "checkout p95 is 2.4 s", "38% of support tickets are password resets"), the target value, and the date by which the target matters. The problem statement MUST NOT contain the proposed solution; "we need to migrate to service X" is a solution, not a problem, and is rejected.

rationale.source: Malte Ubl, 'Design Docs at Google' (2020); widely established practice in RFC and design-document writing

rule.rationale: An RFC whose problem is "adopt Kafka" cannot be argued against, because the only alternative to the solution is not doing it. A number and a date give the reviewers something to disagree with, give the options something to be compared on, and give the outcome review something to measure.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `options` listing at least two genuinely different approaches, one of which MAY be "do nothing / keep current behaviour" but at least one other MUST be a real alternative implementation. Every option that is not chosen MUST carry a one-line reason for rejection tied to the problem metric, cost or risk. An RFC with a single option is a task description, not an RFC, and is rejected.

rationale.source: Michael Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions' (2011), the ADR format; Malte Ubl, 'Design Docs at Google' (2020)

rule.rationale: The value of the record six months later is the list of what was not done and why. An RFC with one option records that a decision happened; it does not record the decision. Reviewers who see only one path have nothing to review except the prose.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `blast_radius` listing every service, data store, public or internal API, scheduled job and user segment the change touches, with a count for each user-facing item (percentage of traffic, number of tenants, number of API consumers), and a yes/no for each of: schema change, public API change, data backfill, third-party integration change. `blast_radius: none` or `blast_radius: low` without the list is rejected.

rationale.source: widely established practice in change management and release engineering

rule.rationale: "Low risk" is a feeling; "two services, one shared table, 12% of traffic, no public API change" is a review input. The enumerated list is also what picks the reviewers: every service in it owes an owner's read, and the ones left off the list are the ones that page at 3 a.m.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `rollback` naming the mechanism (feature flag off, revert PR, down-migration, config revert), the time it takes to execute, who can execute it, and whether it was exercised in staging (yes with a run URL, or no with the reason). Any step that cannot be rolled back (destructive migration, customer-visible email, external API call with side effects) MUST be named as the point of no return with the check that runs immediately before it. An RFC with an empty rollback field is rejected.

rationale.source: 'Site Reliability Engineering' (Beyer, Jones, Petoff, Murphy, 2016), chapters on release engineering and managing incidents; widely established practice

rule.rationale: Every change is a bet, and the rollback is the stake. A rollback that exists only as the sentence "we can revert" was never timed, never tried, and turns out to require a data fix nobody has written when the metric spikes at 17:55 on a Friday.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `milestones` with at least two dated checkpoints inside a 3 to 6 week window, each describing a demonstrable increment (something a reviewer can click, query or observe), and the last milestone is the ship date. An estimate above 6 weeks MUST split the work into separate RFCs, each shippable alone; an RFC with a single "done" milestone or with milestones that are phases of activity ("design", "implementation") rather than increments is rejected.

rationale.source: Ryan Singer, 'Shape Up: Stop Running in Circles and Ship Work that Matters' (Basecamp, 2019), on six-week cycles and scope hammering

rule.rationale: Work that does not fit in six weeks fits in never; the estimate is wrong in the way that makes it longer, and a single far-off ship date hides the slip until the last week. Dated increments make the slip visible in week two, when there is still a cycle left to cut scope.

rule.statement: `decision` MUST be one declarative sentence naming the chosen option, and the RFC MUST carry `inputs[]` entries `status` (one of `proposed`, `accepted`, `rejected`, `superseded`) and `decided_on` (ISO date). An RFC in status `superseded` MUST link the successor RFC in `evidence[]`; a successor MUST link back. Editing the decision of an `accepted` RFC in place is forbidden: the change is a new RFC that supersedes it.

rationale.source: Michael Nygard, 'Documenting Architecture Decisions' (2011), the ADR format

rule.rationale: A decision without a status is a proposal that some readers treat as final and others as open. Immutable accepted records plus explicit supersession are what let a new engineer read the chain and know which decision is current, and why the earlier one stopped being right.

rule.statement: The RFC MUST carry an `inputs[]` entry `reviewers` listing named people (`role:handle`) including at least one owner from every service or data store in `blast_radius`, and a `comment_deadline` date at least 3 working days after the RFC is shared. The RFC moves to `accepted` only after each listed reviewer has either commented or the deadline has passed; a channel, team alias or "everyone" in the reviewer list is rejected.

rationale.source: Malte Ubl, 'Design Docs at Google' (2020); widely established practice in engineering review

rule.rationale: An RFC addressed to a channel is read by nobody in particular and approved by silence from everybody. Naming the reviewers from the blast radius is how the team that owns the shared table finds out about the change before the migration runs; the deadline is what stops the RFC from waiting forever on a reviewer who is on leave.

rule.statement: `review.next_review_at` MUST be no later than one cycle (6 weeks) after the final milestone's ship date. At that review the RFC MUST record the problem metric re-measured with the same method as the original `problem` statement, the target, and one of `met`, `partially-met`, `not-met`; the dashboard or query URL goes into `evidence[]`. An RFC whose outcome review restates the delivery ("shipped on time") without the metric fails this rule.

rationale.source: widely established practice in product delivery and continuous improvement

rule.rationale: Shipping is not the outcome; the number moving is. Teams that review delivery instead of results accumulate a history of on-time projects and a problem metric that never changed, and nobody can say which RFCs were worth writing.
